verdicts.trueWording: "vast churning implications invisible to the casual reader"
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, browser UA, 200). Full sentence: "If any piece of text (or elision) in a Gene Wolfe novel could be read to suggest vast churning implications invisible to the casual reader, it has definitely been read that way by someone on the internet." The elision limb is explicit in the parenthetical; Gladstone adds that many such readings "are not wrong."

verdicts.trueWording: "We fumble through darkness, trying to assemble clues by touch."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Sentence stands verbatim, closing the paragraph on narrators who "assert their eidetic memories and perfect recall and utter honesty, and then straight-up lie"; the preceding clause "We rely on the text, and the text alone... even as the text screams out, 'do not trust me!'" carries the claim's 'rather than being told' limb.

verdicts.trueWording: "not indica of 'what's really going on', but rather fingerprints, or the signature, of the author"
verdicts.note: Raw page. Quote verbatim ("Wolfe loves to include winking asides between author and audience."); the signature-vs-story-evidence limb is supported one paragraph later: "some of the clues Wolfe provides are not indica of 'what's really going on', but rather fingerprints, or the signature, of the author." Examples given: wolf-skins/Wolfe-skins, werewolf/where Wolfe.

verdicts.trueWording: "the dense prose, interjecting itself with parentheticals and complicating clauses"
verdicts.note: Raw page. Appears in the list of "everything I associate with Gene Wolfe" immediately after the long Fifth Head of Cerberus excerpt, alongside "the acute attention to detail" and the unreliable narrator.

verdicts.trueWording: "One never feels he let a sentence get away from him; there is an aura of control throughout."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Both limbs in one sentence; the aura-of-control clause is the same sentence's second half, so the claim's second limb is verbatim too.

verdicts.trueWording: "What would otherwise be unwieldy and overbearing sentences are made beautiful by careful word choice and a certain confidence of construction."
verdicts.note: Raw page. The 'otherwise unwieldy' limb is the same sentence's subject ("unwieldy and overbearing"), so every limb is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: "Real people really are unreliable narrators all the time, even if they try to be reliable narrators."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Holland introduces it as Wolfe's own words ("a favorite device of Gene Wolfe, who considered it much truer to life. In his words:"). The claim truncates before "even if they try to be reliable narrators", which does not distort the sense.

verdicts.trueWording: "the scene is peppered with clues to the larger story which is wrapped in mystery"
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the scene reads as ordinary recollection — Holland never characterises it as ordinary or plain; he calls the prose dense, 'sophisticated' and 'mature', with 'acute attention to detail' and an 'intensely psychological focus', and the effect 'vivid and compelling'
verdicts.note: Raw page. Quotation is verbatim. The clue-planting limb is fully supported; the contrastive limb is the researcher's addition. Holland does frame the excerpt as recollection ("the slow breakthrough of recollection") but never as ordinary or unremarkable — if anything he flags it as distinctively Wolfean ("in even more Gene Wolfe fashion").

verdicts.trueWording: "There are no obvious genre trappings in this opening paragraph, at all."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Verbatim, in the section headed "What can an opening teach you?", reinforced by "There is nothing speculative, or even particularly fanciful happening here." One framing wrinkle short of a PARTIAL: the essay describes itself as dissecting "a single paragraph" rather than a sentence-by-sentence reading, but it is a close reading of that opening paragraph's own sentences, so the 'sentence-level' descriptor is not a false limb.

verdicts.trueWording: "What's noticeable here is not what's present but what's missing."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Verbatim with curly apostrophe; it opens the paragraph that then names the missing genre trappings.

verdicts.trueWording: "grounded in a narrator's spatial description that is concrete (the orientation of the house) and sensory"
verdicts.note: Raw page. Quote verbatim. The wings/courtyard limb is carried by the opening paragraph Alex reproduces on the same page ("our dormitory was in the east wing of the house, with a broad window facing the central courtyard and thus looking west") and by Alex's own "the house has not just rooms but wings and a courtyard"; his gloss for the orientation is "(the orientation of the house)".

verdicts.trueWording: "Wolfe grasps that weird details feel all the weirder when they are grounded amidst the mundane and the conventional."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Quote verbatim as a substring; the 'among mundane ones' limb is the same sentence's tail. Context is the father's crippled monkey, "Something odd in an otherwise very conventional description of a boyhood home."

verdicts.trueWording: "These little opacities feel 'realer' than any explanation of them would."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Verbatim with curly quotes, closing the essay; preceded by "For Wolfe, 'showing vs. telling' is often a false binary."

verdicts.trueWording: "They hint at a private life that the reader never gets access to."
verdicts.note: Raw page. Verbatim as a substring; the antecedent is explicit — "The soundless gestures the brothers use to share their stories, which closes the paragraph, are never elaborated upon or explained subsequently."

verdicts.trueWording: "they hit at the level of rhythm and structure"
verdicts.note: Raw page. Verbatim inside "Not just because they hit at the level of rhythm and structure, but because so many of them feel like a mystagogic initiation." The 'not just' is additive, not a denial, so the claim's limb holds; note Sini's larger point is the mystagogic quality he calls "vibrational precision".
